hook: The lights they navigate by are mostly gone.
caption:
The lights they navigate by are mostly gone.

Most migrating birds fly at night, using the stars to orient themselves across continents their ancestors crossed for thousands of generations. Eighty percent of the North American sky is now washed out by artificial skyglow, so they navigate through a permanent dawn with no real stars in it. When a flock hits a lit city in fog they circle the glow for hours, calling in the dark and burning through fat reserves, and by morning the sidewalks beneath office buildings collect the bodies; Cornell's latest estimate puts bird-window collisions at roughly one billion a year in the United States alone. A handful of cities now run Lights Out programs during peak spring and fall migration, turning off non-essential exterior lighting, but participation is voluntary and most buildings stay lit.
